extracted.intended_audience: the higher and middle classes; educated Christians and fellow‑Englishmen
extracted.subtask_description: Composing/assessing a moral-religious address (a 'lay sermon') aimed at the higher and middle social classes, blending biblical exegesis, political commentary, and ethical exhortation. Emphasis on practical principles, duties of educated citizens, and philosophical terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation / Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The most general term of the speculative intellect, distinguished from acts of the will: 'representation, or (still better) presentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the umbrella concept under which the following more specific forms (sensation, perception, intuition, conception, etc.) fall; the author uses it to ground his nomenclature and to clarify subsequent distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscious presentation which, if it refers exclusively to the subject as a modification of his own state of being, is a sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensation = subjective change; used to distinguish inward feelings from outward-directed presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscious presentation which, if it refers to an object, is a perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception = awareness of external object; contrasted with sensation (subject-focused) and used as basis for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: A perception immediate and individual is an intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition denotes singular, direct apprehension of an object (a sensible intuition) as opposed to mediated or general cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A perception mediate and by means of a character or mark common to several things is a conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception involves abstraction/generalization (the common mark) and is distinguished from immediate intuition; it underlies general terms and classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact / Cognition (sensuous conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception extrinsic and sensuous is a fact, or a cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a conception remains tied to sensory, extrinsic particulars, it functions as empirical cognition or fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notion
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception purely mental and abstracted from the forms of the understanding itself = a notion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A notion is an internal, abstracted mental construct rather than a sensuous or empirical conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is neither a sensation nor a perception, neither individual nor general, neither referring to outward facts nor abstracted from forms of perception, but an educt of the imagination actuated by pure reason; it lacks an adequate correspondent in the world of the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideas occupy the highest philosophical problem: whether they are merely regulative (Aristotle/Kant) or constitutive and one with the power of Nature (Plato/Plotinus). The distinction matters for the role of abstract thought in moral and metaphysical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual consciousness of ultimate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The mark of higher station is an habitual consciousness of the ultimate principles to which one's opinions are traceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion demands that educated persons can identify and live by the foundational principles behind their beliefs and actions—it's more than common sense or honesty and should be visible in conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to give a reason for one's faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in higher station must 'give to thyself a reason for the faith that is in thee'—i.e., be able to justify their beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both intellectual and moral: ministers of conscience should not be blind followers of custom but should be prepared to explain and defend their convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits of reflection proportional to leisure and position
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits of reflection should at least equal your opportunities of leisure and immunity from bodily labour; attention to moral and public objects should be proportional to the elevation that diversifies your prospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The privileged have a duty to use their leisure for thoughtful reflection about public and private good; neglect here is inexcusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not a blind follower of custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow the 'spirit-ta of custom' blindly; avoid being guided only by fashion or unexamined traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes conformity and urges independent moral reasoning—particularly important for those 'defended against the stings' of future temptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erudition as ornament, not universal duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Erudition is an ornament that beseems high station but is a professional task only and not a universal duty for all in elevated life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While learning is admirable, it is not required of every person in high station unless their profession demands it; moral consciousness and reflection are more broadly required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplate particulars in their universal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemplating particulars in their universal laws tends to fix and liberalize the morality of private life and to produce enlightened public zeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a methodological and moral prescription: study particulars within larger principles to improve personal virtue and public policy; it also recalls generosity's original meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout argumentation and conduct one should guard against extremes of all kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly frames moderation as essential, promising to avoid extreme positions in religious and moral matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist in hopeful, faith-based action ('sow beside all waters')
rubrics_metrics.description: Continue morally useful action (to 'sow beside all waters') even when reason or circumstance tempts despair; faith justifies persevering efforts for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exhortation to courageous, hopeful public conduct: do the right things despite apparent futility because prophetic promise and moral duty require it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Scripture as elements of public prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bible presents the means and conditions of spiritual convalescence and also serves as elements of public prudence—teaching causes, preventives, and cures of public evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defends using scriptural authorities (e.g., prophets, inspired poets and historians) as guides for statesmanship and moral policy; they form a repository of precedents and principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑question diagnostic framework for national distress
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating public distress ask three questions: (1) Who has prescribed and what are their qualifications and conduct? (2) What is the true seat and source of the complaint (ultimate as well as immediate causes)? (3) What are the appropriate medicines (who are the true physicians)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rubric structures political-moral diagnosis and prescribes careful examination of agents, causes, and remedies before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish opinions without principle from unprincipled opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate mere opinions lacking principles with opinions that are unprincipled; the former may be harmless if not followed by action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction implies different moral responses: bad principles require correction; opinions without principle require cultivation of habits preventing harm.
